interview_metadata.name: Adam Clark
interview_metadata.protocol: American Voices Project (Park et al. 2024, Table 7) — Full 109 questions

transcript.question_text: To start, I would like to begin with a big question: tell me the story of your life. Start from the beginning -- from your childhood, to education, to family and relationships, and to any major life events you may have had.
transcript.response: I was born in Milwaukee, Wisconsin, and grew up in a middle-class Midwestern family where being reliable mattered a lot. My dad worked in manufacturing operations and my mom worked as an office administrator, so our house was pretty practical: do your homework, show up on time, help your neighbors, keep things in order. I was the kid who liked taking apart the family desktop and then getting nervous until I put it back together correctly. By high school I was into computers, history books, and running, though I was never the loudest person in the room. I went to college and earned a bachelor's degree in computer science, and that gave me a clear direction. After graduation I worked my way through a couple of software jobs, first doing backend Java work and then more full-stack development with Python, React, Node, and SQL. I moved to South Florida for work opportunities and ended up staying because Hollywood felt like a good balance: coastal, busy enough, but still manageable if you build routines. I met my wife through mutual friends, and our relationship has been one of the most stabilizing parts of my life. We do not have kids right now, but we have a pretty full household rhythm between work, exercise, cooking, friends, and family visits. A major life event for me was deciding to stay in software after a rough early job where I nearly burned out; instead of leaving the field, I found a better team and learned how much healthy engineering culture matters. These days I see myself as a steady, routine-oriented person trying to grow into technical leadership while still protecting time for my marriage, health, and community.

follow_ups.question: What were your weekdays like when you were growing up?
follow_ups.response: Pretty structured. School, homework at the kitchen table, dinner around 6:30, and then maybe TV or tinkering with the computer if I had finished what I needed to do.

follow_ups.question: Who shaped you the most as a kid?
follow_ups.response: My parents, mostly. My dad modeled consistency and my mom was the one who kept people connected, remembered birthdays, organized family meals, that kind of thing.

transcript.question_text: Some people tell us that they've reached a crossroads at some points in their life where multiple paths were available, and their choice then made a significant difference in defining who they are. What about you? Was there a moment like that for you, and if so, could you tell me the whole story about that from start to finish?
transcript.response: The biggest crossroads was probably in my late twenties. I was at a software job where everything was rushed, documentation was weak, and security was treated like something you patched on later. I was working late, eating badly, and starting to think maybe I had picked the wrong career. Around that time, a senior developer pulled me aside after a production issue and basically said, 'You are good at this, but you need to choose the kind of engineer you want to be.' That stuck with me. I interviewed for a smaller company with a healthier process, took a slight short-term pay tradeoff, and rebuilt my confidence. That decision made me value maintainable code, testing, mentoring, and not burning people out. It also influenced my current goal of becoming a technical lead rather than just chasing whatever title pays the most.

follow_ups.question: What made the old job so hard day to day?
follow_ups.response: Constant emergency fixes. I would get Slack messages at night, dig through legacy code with no tests, and feel like every fix might break something else.

follow_ups.question: How did your wife or friends respond when you made the change?
follow_ups.response: My wife was supportive and practical. She asked what our budget would look like and told me she would rather see me come home calmer than keep grinding like that.

transcript.question_text: Some people tell us they made a conscious choice or decision in moments like these, while others say it 'just happened'. What about you?
transcript.response: It was a conscious choice. I made a spreadsheet, compared pay, commute, benefits, and growth, and decided that a healthier engineering environment was worth more than a small raise.

follow_ups.question: Did you talk it through with anyone before deciding?
follow_ups.response: Yes, with my wife and one former coworker I trusted.

follow_ups.question: Did you second-guess it afterward?
follow_ups.response: For the first month, yes. After my sleep improved, I knew it was the right call.

transcript.question_text: Do you think another person or an organization could have lent a helping hand during moments like this?
transcript.response: A better manager could have helped earlier. Even basic mentoring, realistic deadlines, and a stronger code review process would have made that workplace less chaotic.

follow_ups.question: What kind of help would have mattered most?
follow_ups.response: Clear priorities and protection from constant context switching.

follow_ups.question: Has that changed how you mentor others?
follow_ups.response: Definitely. I try to give junior developers context, not just tickets.

transcript.question_text: Moving to present time, tell me more about family who are important to you. Do you have a partner, or children?
transcript.response: I am married. My wife is the person I spend the most time with and the person who keeps me from getting too locked into work mode. We do not have children right now. Our life is pretty centered on the two of us: weekday dinners, grocery runs, checking in about work, and trying to keep weekends from getting swallowed by chores. We cook together a lot, especially Sunday meals, and I usually handle anything involving the grill or cast-iron skillet. My parents are still important to me even though they do not live nearby; we talk by phone and see each other around holidays when travel works. I also have a sister I keep in touch with, mostly by text and occasional video calls. Family for me is not dramatic, it is more about showing up consistently.

follow_ups.question: What does a normal evening with your wife look like?
follow_ups.response: We usually eat around 7, clean up together, then maybe watch an episode of something or I read while she catches up with friends.

follow_ups.question: Do relatives visit you in Hollywood?
follow_ups.response: A few times a year. My parents like visiting in winter, and we usually take them to the beach or out for Cuban food.

transcript.question_text: Are there anyone else in your immediate family whom you have not mentioned? Who are they, and what is your relationship with them like?
transcript.response: My parents and my younger sister are the main ones. We are close in a steady way, not talking every day, but we check in and show up for holidays and major decisions.

follow_ups.question: How often do you talk with your sister?
follow_ups.response: Usually a couple times a month by text, more if something is going on.

follow_ups.question: Are family holidays important?
follow_ups.response: Yes, especially Thanksgiving and the Fourth of July.

transcript.question_text: Tell me about anyone else in your life we haven't discussed (like friends or romantic partners). Are there people outside of your family who are important to you?
transcript.response: I have a small but solid group of friends. Some are from work, some are from the Hollywood Beach jogging club, and a couple are board game friends we see maybe twice a month. We play Terraforming Mars, Pandemic, or something strategic, and people bring snacks or beer. I also ride with the Broward County Bike Group on weekends when my schedule lines up. I am not someone with fifty casual friends, but I value the people I can count on.

follow_ups.question: Who do you see most often outside your household?
follow_ups.response: Probably two friends from the jogging group and one coworker I grab lunch with.

follow_ups.question: Where do you usually meet friends?
follow_ups.response: Beachfront runs, local breweries, our house for board games, or sometimes a casual Cuban restaurant nearby.

transcript.question_text: Now let's talk about your current neighborhood. Tell me all about the neighborhood and area in which you are living now.
transcript.response: I live in Hollywood, Florida, in the 33021 area, which is more residential than the tourist image people have of Hollywood Beach. There are single-family homes, condos, shopping plazas, parks, and a mix of longtime residents and newer people. I like that I can get to the beach for a run, but my day-to-day neighborhood still feels practical: grocery stores, gyms, coffee, hardware stores, and decent restaurants. The area has a real South Florida mix, including Cuban and Latin food, retirees, working families, and people commuting around Broward and Miami-Dade. Traffic can be frustrating, especially around I-95 or beach routes, but I like the balance overall.

follow_ups.question: What places do you go to most often near home?
follow_ups.response: Publix, the gym, a local coffee shop, the community center, and the beach broadwalk when I run.

follow_ups.question: Do you know your neighbors?
follow_ups.response: A few by name. We wave, talk after storms, and keep an eye out for packages.

transcript.question_text: Some people say they feel really safe in their neighborhoods, others not so much. How about for you?
transcript.response: I generally feel safe. I am aware of car break-ins and I would not leave a bike unlocked, but I feel comfortable walking in the evening and running early.

follow_ups.question: Do you take any precautions?
follow_ups.response: I lock the car, keep lights on outside, and avoid leaving gear visible.

follow_ups.question: Has anything happened personally?
follow_ups.response: Nothing major, just hearing about petty theft nearby.

transcript.question_text: Living any place has its ups and downs. Tell me about what it's been like for you living here.
transcript.response: The ups are weather, beach access, food, and a laid-back pace. The downs are insurance costs, traffic, summer humidity, and hurricane preparation every year.

follow_ups.question: What is your favorite part of living there?
follow_ups.response: Early runs by the beach before the crowds show up.

follow_ups.question: What is the biggest hassle?
follow_ups.response: Home insurance and storm season planning.

transcript.question_text: Tell me about the people who live with you right now, even people who are staying here temporarily.
transcript.response: Right now it is just me and my wife living in our home. We split household responsibilities pretty evenly, though I tend to do grilling, tech troubleshooting, and yard or storm-prep tasks. She handles some planning that I would probably over-engineer, like social plans and appointments. We do not have children, lodgers, or anyone temporarily staying with us.

follow_ups.question: How do you split chores during a typical week?
follow_ups.response: We both cook and clean; I usually do trash, repairs, grilling, and bills tracking.

follow_ups.question: Do you have pets?
follow_ups.response: No pets right now.

transcript.question_text: Is anyone in your household a temporary member, or is everyone a permanent member of the household?
transcript.response: Everyone is permanent. It is just my wife and me.

follow_ups.question: No one staying for work or school?
follow_ups.response: No.

follow_ups.question: Any long-term guests expected?
follow_ups.response: Not at the moment.

transcript.question_text: Tell me about anyone else who stays here from time to time, if there is anyone like that
transcript.response: Family may stay for a holiday visit, but not regularly.

follow_ups.question: Who visits most often?
follow_ups.response: My parents, usually in winter.

follow_ups.question: How long do they stay?
follow_ups.response: Usually a few days.

transcript.question_text: Is there anyone who usually lives here but is away -- traveling, at school, or in a hospital?
transcript.response: No, nobody is away from the household.

follow_ups.question: So the household count is two?
follow_ups.response: Yes, two.

follow_ups.question: Any college students tied to the home?
follow_ups.response: No.

transcript.question_text: Right now, across a typical week, how do your days vary?
transcript.response: Monday through Friday I am pretty structured. I usually wake up around 6, run or do a short workout a few mornings, start work around 8:30, and finish around 5:30 or 6 unless there is a deployment. Tuesdays are strength training days. Friday night is usually classic movie night at home, often something like Casablanca or The Maltese Falcon. Saturdays are for a longer bike ride if weather cooperates, errands, and sometimes board games with friends. Sundays are meal prep, laundry, maybe smoking ribs or making shrimp and grits, and checking my calendar for the week.

follow_ups.question: What time do you usually exercise?
follow_ups.response: Early, usually between 6:15 and 7:15 in the morning.

follow_ups.question: What is the most protected routine?
follow_ups.response: Sunday planning and Friday movie night. Those keep the week from feeling scattered.

transcript.question_text: At what kind of job or jobs do you work, and when do you work?
transcript.response: I work full time as a full-stack software developer. My work is a mix of Java and Python backend services, React frontends, SQL databases, code reviews, bug fixing, and mentoring junior engineers. My normal hours are business hours, roughly 8:30 to 5:30, Monday through Friday, with some flexibility because part of the team works remotely. I also have a small side consultancy idea that brings in occasional work for local small businesses, but I am careful not to let that take over evenings.

follow_ups.question: Where do you work from most days?
follow_ups.response: Mostly from home with some office days or client meetings when needed.

follow_ups.question: What part of the job do you like most?
follow_ups.response: Refactoring something messy into code that other people can understand and maintain.

transcript.question_text: Do you have other routines or responsibilities that you did not already share?
transcript.response: Once a month I volunteer at a local community center teaching basic coding to middle school students. I also keep a pretty close eye on household finances, insurance renewals, and hurricane supplies. My wife and I do a Sunday grocery plan so weeknights do not turn into takeout every night. I also spend a few hours a week studying for AWS certification.

follow_ups.question: What do you teach at the community center?
follow_ups.response: Basic Scratch, simple web pages, and how to think through problems step by step.

follow_ups.question: When do you study for AWS?
follow_ups.response: Usually two evenings a week, about 45 minutes at a time.

transcript.question_text: Tell me about any recent changes to your daily routine.
transcript.response: The main recent change is being more deliberate about health tracking. I started using a watch to monitor sleep, resting heart rate, and workout consistency. I also shifted some side consultancy work away from weeknights because it was making me too wired before bed. At work, I have been mentoring more, which means more meetings and fewer uninterrupted coding blocks.

follow_ups.question: What did you cut back first?
follow_ups.response: Late-night client work. It hurt my sleep too much.

follow_ups.question: Has the health tracking helped?
follow_ups.response: Yes, mostly because it makes patterns obvious. I cannot pretend five hours of sleep is fine.

transcript.question_text: If you have children, tell me about a typical weekday during the school year for your children. What is their daily routine? And what are after school activities your children participate in?
transcript.response: We do not have children, so I do not have a school-year routine for kids. The closest thing is my monthly coding volunteer work with middle school students.

follow_ups.question: Do children factor into your future plans?
follow_ups.response: We have talked about it, but we have not made a firm decision.

follow_ups.question: Do you spend time with nieces, nephews, or friends' kids?
follow_ups.response: Occasionally with friends' kids at gatherings, but not as a regular caregiving role.

transcript.question_text: Some people we've talked to tell us about experiences with law enforcement. How about for you?
transcript.response: My personal experiences have been limited and mostly routine. I have had traffic stops, including one speeding warning years ago and one ticket. In Hollywood I mostly see police around traffic accidents, beach events, or storm situations. I have not had a serious negative encounter myself, but I know that is not everyone's experience.

follow_ups.question: How did those traffic stops feel?
follow_ups.response: Nerve-racking but straightforward. I handed over my license, answered clearly, and it ended quickly.

follow_ups.question: Do police have a visible presence in your area?
follow_ups.response: Yes, especially around bigger events, busy roads, and after storms.

transcript.question_text: What other experiences with law enforcement stand out in your mind?
transcript.response: After a hurricane scare, seeing police and fire crews coordinate road closures stood out. It made me appreciate emergency planning, even if traffic control was frustrating.

follow_ups.question: Have you ever called police yourself?
follow_ups.response: No, not for anything serious.

follow_ups.question: Any workplace contact with law enforcement?
follow_ups.response: No, not in my software work.

transcript.question_text: Some people tell us about experiences of arrest -- of loved ones, family members, friends, or themselves. How about for you?
transcript.response: I have never been arrested, and no immediate family member has been arrested as far as I know. I have known acquaintances with DUIs, but not close family.

follow_ups.question: Did those acquaintances' situations affect you?
follow_ups.response: Mostly as a reminder not to be careless after drinking.

follow_ups.question: Any legal expenses tied to that?
follow_ups.response: No, nothing involving me or my household.

transcript.question_text: Some people say they vote in every election, some tell us they don't vote at all. How about you?
transcript.response: I vote regularly, especially in presidential and midterm elections. I also try to vote in local elections because city and county decisions affect things like roads, development, schools, and storm preparation. I am not the loudest political person online, but I take voting seriously. I usually read a sample ballot ahead of time and look up judicial and local races.

follow_ups.question: Do you vote early, by mail, or on Election Day?
follow_ups.response: Usually early voting. It fits my planning style.

follow_ups.question: Do you discuss your vote with family?
follow_ups.response: Sometimes with my wife and parents, but I avoid turning holidays into debates.

transcript.question_text: How would you describe your political views?
transcript.response: I would describe myself as moderate, pragmatic, and slightly center-left overall. I care about competent government, infrastructure, public education, health care access, and environmental planning, especially living in South Florida with flooding and hurricane risks. On economic issues I am not anti-business at all; I work in tech and understand that small businesses need room to operate. But I also think basic safeguards matter, whether that is consumer protection, cybersecurity standards, or a health system that does not punish people for getting sick. Socially I am pretty live-and-let-live. I am skeptical of political extremes and performative outrage from either side. I vote more often for Democrats lately, but I would rather evaluate the candidate and the office than treat party as a team sport.

follow_ups.question: What issues shape your vote most?
follow_ups.response: Competence, climate resilience, health care, education, and whether someone seems serious about governing.

follow_ups.question: Do your coworkers share similar views?
follow_ups.response: Some do, but tech workplaces can be a mix. I keep political talk measured at work.

transcript.question_text: Tell me about any recent changes in your political views.
transcript.response: I have become more focused on local governance and less patient with national political theater. Living in Florida makes issues like insurance, storm resilience, housing costs, and infrastructure feel very concrete. I have also become more concerned about misinformation and cybersecurity because I see how technical systems can be exploited. I am probably more pro-institution than I was when I was younger, but only when institutions are transparent and accountable.

follow_ups.question: What made local politics feel more important?
follow_ups.response: Seeing how insurance rates, zoning, drainage, and emergency planning affect normal household budgets.

follow_ups.question: Has your party preference changed?
follow_ups.response: I have drifted somewhat more Democratic, but I still think of myself as moderate.

transcript.question_text: One topic a lot of people have been talking about recently is race and/or racism and policing. Some tell us issues raised by the Black Lives Matter movement have affected them a lot, some say they've affected them somewhat, others say they haven't affected them at all. How about for you?
transcript.response: I would say they affected me somewhat. As a white guy who has had mostly routine experiences with police, I know my perspective is limited. The conversations around Black Lives Matter made me listen more closely to coworkers, neighbors, and friends whose experiences were different from mine. I would not say it reshaped my entire identity, but it did make me more aware of how uneven people's day-to-day interactions with institutions can be.

follow_ups.question: Where did you hear those perspectives?
follow_ups.response: Mostly from friends, coworkers, podcasts, local news, and some community conversations.

follow_ups.question: Did it change any behavior?
follow_ups.response: It made me slower to dismiss people's concerns and more likely to ask what policy change is actually being proposed.

transcript.question_text: How have you been thinking about the issues Black Lives Matter raises?
transcript.response: I think the underlying issues are real: accountability, use of force, trust, and unequal treatment. I also think slogans can flatten complicated policy discussions, so I try to look past the loudest version of the debate. I support better training, body cameras, transparency around complaints, and community-based responses for certain situations. I am not anti-police, but I do think public authority should come with strong oversight.

follow_ups.question: What policy sounds most practical to you?
follow_ups.response: Transparent complaint tracking and better crisis response options.

follow_ups.question: Do you talk about this at work?
follow_ups.response: Only carefully, usually if someone else raises it in a thoughtful way.

transcript.question_text: How have you been thinking about race in the U.S. recently?
transcript.response: I think about it as something that is both historical and very current. Growing up in the Midwest, I was taught the basic civil rights history, but adulthood has made me more aware of housing, schools, wealth, and policing as systems that still shape outcomes. In South Florida you also see many ethnic and cultural communities living close together, which is a strength but does not mean everything is equal. I try to be honest that I still have blind spots.

follow_ups.question: Has living in South Florida changed your perspective?
follow_ups.response: Yes. The diversity is more visible day to day, and it makes national categories feel less simple.

follow_ups.question: How do you keep learning?
follow_ups.response: Reading, listening to people I know, and not relying only on social media arguments.

transcript.question_text: How have you responded to the increased focus on race and/or racism and policing? Some people tell us they're aware of the issue but keep their thoughts to themselves, others say they've talked to family and friends, others have joined protests. What about you?
transcript.response: I have mostly talked with family and friends and tried to listen. I have not joined protests, but I have voted with these issues in mind and supported accountability-focused local candidates.

follow_ups.question: Were those conversations difficult?
follow_ups.response: Sometimes, especially with older relatives who see the issue differently.

follow_ups.question: Do you post about it online?
follow_ups.response: Rarely. I do not think social media is where I am most useful.

transcript.question_text: What about people you're close to? How have they responded to the increased focus on race and/or racism and policing?
transcript.response: My wife is thoughtful about it and probably more willing than I am to talk about the human side first. Some friends are very engaged, while others are tired of political conflict and avoid the topic. My parents are more cautious and tend to worry that criticism of policing becomes too broad. I try to keep those conversations grounded in specific reforms rather than accusations.

follow_ups.question: Has this caused tension?
follow_ups.response: A little, but not serious family rupture.

follow_ups.question: Who influences your thinking most?
follow_ups.response: My wife and a couple coworkers who are measured and informed.

transcript.question_text: Now we'd like to learn more about your health. First, tell me all about your health.
transcript.response: Overall my health is good. I jog, cycle, and lift on Tuesdays, and I try to keep my weight and blood pressure in a healthy range. I monitor sleep and heart rate more than I used to. My weak spots are stress, sitting too long during work, and overdoing barbecue or fried food when I am experimenting in the kitchen.

follow_ups.question: Do you have any chronic conditions?
follow_ups.response: No major chronic diagnosis.

follow_ups.question: How often do you exercise?
follow_ups.response: Usually four or five days a week between running, cycling, and strength training.

transcript.question_text: For you, what makes it easy or hard to stay healthy?
transcript.response: Routine makes it easy. If I run early, meal plan, and go to bed on time, I do fine. What makes it hard is deadline pressure, late screen time, summer heat, and the fact that I genuinely enjoy ribs, fried chicken, and shrimp and grits.

follow_ups.question: What is your healthiest habit?
follow_ups.response: Morning exercise before work.

follow_ups.question: What habit slips first?
follow_ups.response: Sleep, then food choices.

transcript.question_text: Tell me about anything big that has happened in the past two years related to your health: any medical diagnoses, flare-ups of chronic conditions, broken bones, pain -- anything like that.
transcript.response: Nothing major like a diagnosis or broken bone. I had some lower back tightness from sitting and a mild knee irritation after increasing mileage too quickly. Physical therapy exercises and being more sensible about running volume helped. My annual checkup was mostly normal, with the usual advice to keep an eye on cholesterol and not let work stress creep up.

follow_ups.question: Did the knee issue stop your running?
follow_ups.response: I cut back for a few weeks and cycled more instead.

follow_ups.question: Did you see a doctor?
follow_ups.response: I brought it up at a checkup and used recommended stretching and strengthening exercises.

transcript.question_text: Sometimes, health problems get in the way. They can even affect people's ability to work or care for their children. How about you?
transcript.response: My health has not seriously interfered with work. The main issue is that poor sleep or back tightness can make coding and meetings feel harder, so I try to address it early.

follow_ups.question: Have you missed work for health reasons?
follow_ups.response: Only normal sick days.

follow_ups.question: Do you need accommodations?
follow_ups.response: No formal accommodations.

transcript.question_text: Sometimes, it's not your health problem, but the health of a loved one. Has this been an issue for you?
transcript.response: Somewhat. My parents are getting older, and while they are generally independent, I think more about their health now. There have been routine issues like blood pressure, dental work, and helping them understand insurance paperwork. My wife and I are healthy, but we have both had moments where stress made us realize we need to slow down.

follow_ups.question: Do you provide direct caregiving?
follow_ups.response: Not daily, but I help with research, calls, and planning when my parents need it.

follow_ups.question: Does distance make that harder?
follow_ups.response: Yes. Phone support only goes so far.

transcript.question_text: Tell me what it has been like trying to get the health care you or your immediate family need. Have you ever had to forgo getting the health care you need?
transcript.response: We have employer health insurance, so we are in a better position than many people. The frustrating parts are scheduling specialists, figuring out what is in network, and getting surprise-ish bills that are technically explained but still annoying. I have not had to forgo necessary care, but I have delayed minor things because appointments were inconvenient or the cost was unclear.

follow_ups.question: Who handles insurance details at home?
follow_ups.response: I usually track the paperwork and compare costs.

follow_ups.question: What kind of care gets delayed?
follow_ups.response: Minor physical therapy follow-ups or nonurgent appointments.

transcript.question_text: Have you or your immediate family ever used alternative forms of medicine? This might include indigenous, non-western, or informal forms of care.
transcript.response: Nothing major or deeply alternative. We use stretching, massage, heat packs, and the occasional herbal tea or supplement, but we still rely on regular doctors and evidence-based care. My wife has tried yoga for stress and flexibility, and I think that helps. I am cautious about anything that sounds like it replaces medical care.

follow_ups.question: Do you take supplements?
follow_ups.response: A basic multivitamin sometimes, but not a big stack.

follow_ups.question: Would you try acupuncture or similar care?
follow_ups.response: Maybe for pain, but I would research it first.

transcript.question_text: During tough times, some people tell us they cope by smoking or drinking. How about for you?
transcript.response: I do not smoke. I drink socially, usually a beer with friends, a drink at a brewery, or wine with dinner, but not every night. During tough times I am more likely to run, cook, or get quiet than drink heavily. I am aware that using alcohol for stress can sneak up on people, so I try not to make that my pattern.

follow_ups.question: How many drinks in a typical week?
follow_ups.response: Usually two to four, sometimes none.

follow_ups.question: What do you do when stress spikes?
follow_ups.response: Run, take a walk, make a list, or talk with my wife.

transcript.question_text: Other people say they cope by relying on prescriptions, pain medications, marijuana, or other substances. How about for you and can you describe your most recent experience of using them, if any?
transcript.response: I do not use marijuana or other recreational drugs. I use over-the-counter pain relievers occasionally, like ibuprofen after a sore run or for a headache. The most recent time was after a longer bike ride when my knee felt irritated; I took ibuprofen, iced it, and skipped running the next day. I do not take prescription medications for mood or pain.

follow_ups.question: Any concern about pain medication use?
follow_ups.response: No, it is occasional and pretty minimal.

follow_ups.question: Do people around you use marijuana?
follow_ups.response: Some friends do occasionally, but it is not my thing.

transcript.question_text: How are you and your family coping with, or paying for, your health care needs right now?
transcript.response: We pay through employer-sponsored insurance, payroll deductions, copays, and an HSA-style savings cushion for medical costs. I try to keep enough cash set aside for deductibles or dental surprises. It is manageable for us, but I still find the system too complicated. For my parents, I sometimes help them compare plan information or understand bills.

follow_ups.question: Do health costs affect your budget?
follow_ups.response: They do, but they are planned for rather than a crisis right now.

follow_ups.question: Do you skip preventive care?
follow_ups.response: No, I try to keep up with annual checkups and dental cleanings.

transcript.question_text: Some people are excited about medical vaccination, and others, not so much. How about you?
transcript.response: I am pro-vaccination. I got COVID vaccines and boosters when recommended, and I get a flu shot most years. I see it as basic risk reduction.

follow_ups.question: Was that an easy decision?
follow_ups.response: Yes, after reading reliable sources.

follow_ups.question: Any side effects?
follow_ups.response: Just a sore arm and fatigue for a day.

transcript.question_text: What are your trusted sources of information about the vaccine?
transcript.response: I trust my primary care doctor, CDC guidance, major hospital systems, and medical experts who explain uncertainty clearly. I also look for consensus rather than one viral post. I am technical enough to know that data can be misread, so I try not to overestimate my ability to interpret medical studies from scratch.

follow_ups.question: Do you use social media for vaccine information?
follow_ups.response: No, not as a primary source.

follow_ups.question: Do friends ask you tech-style research questions about it?
follow_ups.response: Sometimes, and I usually point them to doctors or official sources.

transcript.question_text: We all have hopes about what our future will look like. Imagine yourself a few years from now. Maybe you want your life to be the same in some ways as it is now. Maybe you want it to be different in some ways. What do you hope for?
transcript.response: A few years from now, I hope my life still has the stable parts I value: a strong marriage, good health, close friends, and routines that keep me grounded. Professionally, I hope to be a senior engineer or technical lead, someone who shapes standards and helps teams build reliable systems without burning out. I want to finish the AWS certification and lead cloud migration work, maybe for local businesses through a carefully managed consultancy. I also hope my wife and I have clarity about family plans, whether that means children or building a meaningful life as a couple without them. Personally, I want more travel, especially a quiet Iceland trip, but not at the expense of financial stability. I want to stay useful in the community, keep volunteering, and be the kind of person people can rely on.

follow_ups.question: What would success look like at work?

follow_ups.question: What do you want to protect from changing?

transcript.question_text: What do you value the most in your life?
transcript.response: I value responsibility, stability, honesty, and the people closest to me. My marriage comes first, then family, health, meaningful work, and community. I also value competence, which sounds dry, but to me it means caring enough to do things well. Whether it is code, cooking dinner, helping a student, or preparing for hurricane season, I respect people who show up and follow through.

follow_ups.question: Where did those values come from?
follow_ups.response: Mostly my parents and the Midwestern way I was raised.

follow_ups.question: How do those values show up daily?
follow_ups.response: Planning, keeping commitments, helping at home, and trying to be dependable at work.
